title: In Colombia's Roadless Jungles, Traditional Midwives Are a Lifeline—But They Want Respect
summary: Nohemí Manco was 14 when her sister went into labor in their remote home in Unguía, Colombia—a place of dense jungle, waterfalls, and zero hospitals. With no doctor or ambulance, Manco relied on what she'd absorbed from watching her mother: where to cut the umbilical cord, which teas ease pain, how to care for a newborn. "I loved it. I wasn't even scared," she recalls. Four decades later, Manco, now 53, estimates she has delivered about 1,200 babies. She's part of a vast network of "parteras tradicionales"—traditional midwives—who serve as the primary healthcare providers for pregnant women in Colombia's isolated Pacific region. In these areas, a hospital can be hours or even days away, making midwives crucial to reducing maternal and infant deaths. "Midwives are the main and most constant resource for rural communities," says Liany Katerine Ariza Ruiz, a public health researcher at Pontificia Universidad Javeriana. Yet despite their vital role, many midwives say they face discrimination from Colombia's formal healthcare system. They report being mocked, dismissed, and sometimes barred from hospitals when accompanying patients. "For a while, we felt the tradition was being lost because there was so much discrimination," says Yuvianis Florez, a 36-year-old midwife. A 2026 survey identified at least 1,742 traditional midwives active in the region—11% of them men—but the population is aging rapidly. Nearly half are over 60, and 40% are illiterate. Florez and Manco don't reject modern medicine; they want collaboration. "We want to work together to ensure the safety of rural women," Florez explains. Manco believes midwives can also be advocates for education and reproductive health. As younger generations show less interest, the fight isn't just for respect—it's for survival of a centuries-old tradition that continues to save lives where roads and clinics don't reach.
why_it_matters: This story highlights the challenges of providing healthcare in remote areas and the importance of bridging traditional and modern medicine—a debate that affects rural communities worldwide.

background_read: Unguía is a municipality in the Chocó department of Colombia, a region covered by dense rainforest and lacking roads, making travel to cities extremely difficult.
Traditional midwifery has been practiced for centuries in many parts of the world, especially where formal healthcare is inaccessible; in Colombia, these midwives are called parteras.
The Pontificia Universidad Javeriana (a leading Colombian university founded in 1623) conducts public health research in these remote areas.
Globally, maternal mortality rates are higher in rural regions without skilled birth attendants, which is why the United Nations targets reducing these deaths.
Discrimination against traditional birth attendants is not unique to Colombia; similar tensions between formal health systems and indigenous healers exist in other countries.

perspectives.description: Traditional midwives are essential: they deliver thousands of babies in places with no doctors, drastically lowering the risk of mothers and infants dying alone. Their work is a testament to community resilience and the power of inherited knowledge.

Despite their vital role, midwives face mockery and exclusion from hospitals. This disrespect not only hurts their dignity but can also endanger patients if midwives are denied backup support, showing a failure of the formal system to acknowledge local realities.

With nearly half of the midwives over 60 and high illiteracy rates, the practice is at risk. Without young recruits and formal recognition, centuries of knowledge could disappear, leaving a healthcare vacuum in the jungle.

If collaboration were achieved—combining midwives' community trust with medical training—it could become a model for other remote regions. Integrating midwives into official health strategies could improve maternal health while preserving cultural heritage.
